nt: The pronoun **they** is used in a general sense to refer to people, craftsmen who craft idols, and the pronoun **him** refers to the person who worships the idols. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [which craftsmen made for the worshiper to worship]

The word that the ULT translates as **when** indicates that Yahweh **arises to terrify the earth** at the same time as the people come **into crevices of rocks and into clefts of crags**. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could describe the time relationship more explicitly. Alternate translation: [to come into crevices of rocks and into clefts of crags from the face of the terror of Yahweh and from the splendor of his majesty at the same time that he arises to terrify the earth]

x.ASV: Cease ye from man, whose breath is in his nostrils; for wherein is he to be accounted of?
x.Darby: Cease ye from man, whose breath is in his nostrils; for what account is to be made of him?
x.KJV: Cease ye from man, whose breath is in his nostrils: for wherein is he to be accounted of?
x.YLT: Cease for you from man, Whose breath is in his nostrils, For--in what is he esteemed?

nt: Here, **breath is in his nose** represents the fact that a person is merely mortal and alive only because God sustains him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [who has life only because God breathes into him]

The expression **is he esteemed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [do people esteem him]

Isaiah is using the question form to emphasize that humans are not worthy of trust. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [for he is not worthy of esteem.]
